summary: This RFC specifies an algorithm for generating TCP Initial Sequence Numbers so an off-path attacker is less likely to guess those in use. It revises and obsoletes RFC 1948 and updates RFC 793. It was itself replaced by RFC 9293.

eli5.summary: When two computers start talking, they pick starting numbers. If a stranger can guess them, they can butt in. This explains how to pick numbers that are hard to guess. A newer RFC 9293 replaced it.

questions: how to prevent sequence number attacks
why is tcp sequence number important
subtitle: Preventing attackers from guessing TCP sequence numbers.

tldr.problem: Attackers can hijack TCP connections if they can guess the initial sequence numbers (ISNs) that a TCP stack chooses for new connections, a weakness in the original TCP specification.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies that each TCP connection should use its own sequence number space, with ISN values generated as M + F(connection_id, secret_key), where M is a timer and F is a pseudorandom function. This makes sequence numbers far harder to predict.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was replaced by RFC 9293, which consolidated this algorithm into TCP's main specification. Off-path attacks still require an attacker to know the connection 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port).

today: RFC 6528 is a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 9293, which consolidated this algorithm into the main TCP specification along with other updates. The secure ISN generation method described here is now the standard approach for all TCP implementations.

sections.title: The Sequence Number Attack Problem
sections.content:
For decades, TCP has faced attacks where an off-path attacker (one who cannot see network traffic) tries to hijack a connection by guessing the initial sequence numbers (ISNs) that TCP uses when a connection starts. The attacker can impersonate one party and trick the other into accepting forged data.

The original TCP specification suggested incrementing a global 32-bit ISN generator by 1 roughly every 4 microseconds. In practice, many implementations simply incremented it more often, making ISNs highly predictable. An attacker who knew one ISN could easily predict the next one. RFC 1948 (1996) proposed a solution; this RFC obsoletes RFC 1948 and makes that solution a formal Internet Standard.
sections.eli5: If computers pick their starting numbers in a predictable pattern, an attacker can guess them and fake a conversation. This RFC explains a way to make the numbers much harder to guess.

sections.title: Why Per-Connection Sequence Spaces Work
sections.content:
The key insight is that each TCP connection (identified by its four-tuple of source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port) should have its own sequence number space. Within each space, ISNs still increment as specified in RFC 793, but there is no predictable relationship between the numbering in different spaces.

This approach avoids two common problems: First, it prevents an attacker from predicting a sequence number by observing the sequence numbers of other connections. Second, it preserves the 4.4BSD heuristic that allows a new connection to replace an old one still in the TIME-WAIT state (which is important for applications that frequently reconnect to the same server). Other solutions exist but would require keeping state about dead connections or observing a quiet time, both of which have drawbacks.
sections.eli5: Instead of one global counter, each conversation gets its own counter. The counters are unpredictable to outsiders, but the program remembers them.

sections.title: The ISN Generation Formula
sections.content:
TCP SHOULD generate Initial Sequence Numbers using the formula:

ISN = M + F(localip, localport, remoteip, remoteport, secretkey)

where M is a 4-microsecond timer (as in RFC 793) and F() is a pseudorandom function of the connection 4-tuple and a secret key. F() could be implemented as a cryptographic hash (such as MD5) of the concatenation of the connection identifier and secret data. The security of this approach depends entirely on the secret key. An attacker who knows the hash function but not the key cannot compute F() values without searching the entire key space.

The secret key MUST be at least 128 bits long to be adequately resistant to attacks. The key can be changed periodically (after system boot, after a time interval, or after sufficient use) to limit the exposure if the key is ever compromised. However, changing the key changes the ISN space for reincarnated connections, so implementers must either keep dead connection state or observe a quiet time before such a change.
sections.eli5: The formula mixes a timer with a secret hash of the connection details. Even if an attacker knows the formula, they cannot compute the hash without the secret.

sections.title: Limitations and Threats
sections.content:
Good sequence numbers are not a replacement for cryptographic authentication mechanisms such as IPsec or the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO). They are a defensive measure against off-path attacks. An eavesdropper who can observe initial messages may determine the sequence number state for that connection and could still attempt attacks, though this is a limited threat since such an eavesdropper can already hijack existing connections.

The algorithm may allow an attacker to count the number of systems behind a Network Address Translator (NAT) by establishing multiple connections and observing the number of distinct sequence number spaces. TCP port randomization (RFC 6056) reduces the ability of attackers to guess the four-tuple of a target connection, contributing to mitigation of off-path attacks. In all cases, the attacker must still guess or know the exact four-tuple to target a specific connection.
sections.eli5: This method helps against attackers who do not see your traffic, but it is not a complete protection. Real security requires stronger authentication. Also, knowing a lot of sequence numbers might leak some information about network structure.

sections.title: Trust Relationships and Why This Matters
sections.content:
In the 1980s, many systems used IP address-based authentication for remote access (such as Telnet and the UNIX "r" commands). An attacker who could hijack a TCP connection from a trusted machine could execute commands on a target as if they were from the trusted machine. Although these trust relationships have largely been replaced by cryptographic authentication (SSH, Kerberos), some systems still use IP-based trust for DNS zone transfers and SMTP authentication.

Morris's 1985 attack demonstrated that weak ISN generation made such hijacking trivial if ISNs were predictable. The attacker would open a real connection to observe the target's sequence numbers, then impersonate a trusted machine with a predicted ISN. This RFC ensures that such attacks become very difficult for off-path attackers, protecting both legacy systems and any modern deployments that still rely on address-based access controls.
sections.eli5: Older systems trusted computers by their addresses. Attackers could pretend to be trusted computers if they could guess sequence numbers. This RFC makes that attack much harder.

left.title: RFC 793 (Weak)
left.desc: Global counter increments predictably. An attacker who observed recent ISNs could guess the next one.

right.title: RFC 6528 (Secure)
right.desc: Each connection hashes its 4-tuple with a secret. Attacker cannot predict ISN without knowing the secret key.
